pos: v.t. (to strike repeatedly; to hammer or pound; to dash against)
etymology: Saxon beatan, to strike. One of the plainest verbs in English, and the Authorized Version uses it thirty-six times — for hammering gold, pounding manna, scourging a man's back, storms against a house, and swords remade into ploughs.
biblical_def: Beat is a working word, and Scripture puts it to every kind of labour. It is the craftsman's verb: the gold of the ephod was beaten into thin plates and cut into wires, and the manna was ground in mills or beaten in a mortar (Num 11:8). It is the judicial verb, and the law limits it: “Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee” (Deu 25:3) — even under punishment the man remains thy brother, and the count exists to protect his dignity. It is the storm's verb in the Lord's parable: “the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock” (Mat 7:25) — the beating is identical on both houses, and only the foundation differs. And it is the great eschatological verb of Isaiah: “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more” (Isa 2:4). The same hammering that shapes a weapon can unshape it, and the prophet promises a day when the forge turns the other way.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines beat as to strike repeatedly; to lay on repeated blows; to strike an instrument of music; to break, bruise or pulverize by beating; and to dash or fall on, as water or wind.
webster_full: BEAT, v.t. pret. beat; pp. beat, beaten. [Sax. beatan.]
1. To strike repeatedly; to lay on repeated blows, with a stick, with the hand or fist, or with any instrument.
2. To strike an instrument of music; as, to beat a drum.
3. To break, bruise, comminute or pulverize by beating or pounding, as pepper or spices.
4. To extend by beating, as gold or other malleable substance. 5. To dash or strike against, as water or wind. They shall beat their swords into plowshares. Is. 2.
scriptures: Isaiah 2:4

And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
Matthew 7:25
And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.
Deuteronomy 25:3
Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee.
Numbers 11:8
And the people went about, and gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans, and made cakes of it: and the taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil.
corruption_summary: Isaiah 2:4 is quoted as a programme for present politics, when the prophet gives it as the fruit of the Judge's reign.
corruption_paragraphs: “They shall beat their swords into plowshares” is carved on the wall at the United Nations and quoted in every generation as a mandate for disarmament now. The verse will not carry it alone, because the first half of the sentence supplies the condition: he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people — and only then do the swords go to the forge. Peace in Isaiah is the consequence of a King actually reigning and actually judging, not of nations agreeing among themselves. Strip out the Judge and what remains is a hope with no mechanism, which is why every attempt to produce the second half without the first has ended with the spears back in production.

Deuteronomy 25:3 deserves its own notice, because it shows how Scripture handles a genuinely violent institution. It does not abolish the scourging; it counts the strokes, and it gives a reason that is entirely about the man being beaten — lest thy brother should seem vile unto thee. Punishment has a limit because the offender never stops being a brother, and a society that punishes without limit degrades the punisher as much as the punished. That is a doctrine of justice far older and far sturdier than the modern alternatives, which tend either to deny that punishment is legitimate at all or to forget that it has a ceiling.
roots_summary: Hebrew kathath (H3807), to beat or crush fine; nakah (H5221), to strike; Greek prospipto (G4363), to fall upon; Saxon beatan, to strike.
roots_lines: Hebrew kittethu (H3807) — they shall beat, hammer, crush; Isaiah 2:4, of swords becoming ploughshares.
Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to smite, strike; the verb of Deuteronomy 25:3 and of judicial scourging generally.
Hebrew dakah (H1794) — to crush, beat small; Numbers 11:8, of the manna in the mortar.
Greek prosepesan (G4363) — they fell upon, beat against; Matthew 7:25, of the storm on the house.
Saxon beatan — to strike; Webster's root, unchanged in a thousand years of English.
usage: “Beat their swords into plowshares” — after he shall judge among the nations, not instead of it.
“The winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not” — the beating was the same; the foundation was not.
“Lest… thy brother should seem vile unto thee” — the count protects the man being struck.

pos: v. (employed; put to service; and in the older idiom, accustomed or habituated)
etymology: From use, Latin uti, to employ. The Authorized Version carries two senses that modern English has separated: employed, and was accustomed to — as in so used the young men to do.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses this plain word twenty-one times, and the range is worth noticing because it is almost entirely moral. It is the word for what men habitually do: “the disciples of John and of the Pharisees used to fast” (Mar 2:18) — the older English sense of were accustomed. It is the word for the forbidden arts: Manasseh and the northern kingdom alike “used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger” (2Ki 17:17). It is the word for institutional cruelty: “The people of the land have used oppression, and exercised robbery, and have vexed the poor and needy: yea, they have oppressed the stranger wrongfully” (Eze 22:29) — oppression as a practice, something a nation uses the way a craftsman uses a tool. And it is the word for how God has spoken to His people: “I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets” (Hos 12:10). That last is a striking admission of divine method — God has deliberately used likenesses, figures, and comparisons, through men, because that is how He chose to be understood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines used as employed; accustomed; and notes the participial sense of being habituated or inured to a thing.
webster_full: U'SED, pp. Employed; accustomed.
U'SE, v.t. s as z. [L. utor, usus.]
1. To employ; to handle, hold or move for some purpose.
2. To make use of; to convert to one's service.
3. To accustom; to habituate; to render familiar by practice. So used the young men to do. Judges 14. In this sense it is now chiefly used in the past tense, as, he used to walk.
scriptures: Hosea 12:10
I have also spoken by the prophets, and I have multiplied visions, and used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets.
2 Kings 17:17
And they caused their sons and their daughters to pass through the fire, and used divination and enchantments, and sold themselves to do evil in the sight of the LORD, to provoke him to anger.
Ezekiel 22:29
The people of the land have used oppression, and exercised robbery, and have vexed the poor and needy: yea, they have oppressed the stranger wrongfully.
Mark 2:18
And the disciples of John and of the Pharisees used to fast: and they come and say unto him, Why do the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fast, but thy disciples fast not?
corruption_summary: Hosea 12:10 is pressed to make the prophets mythmakers, as though God's use of figures made the history figurative.
corruption_paragraphs: I have… used similitudes is a favourite text of those who wish the historical narratives of Scripture to be understood as parable — a literary mode rather than a record. The verse says something narrower and more useful: that God employed likenesses through the ministry of the prophets. Hosea himself is a case in point, since his marriage was both a real marriage and a figure of Israel's adultery, and the figure has its force precisely because the history is real. Divine accommodation in language is not divine fiction in fact. The dictionary holds the ordinary Reformed rule: the literal sense is the sense the author intended, which includes figures where figures are used and history where history is written.

2 Kings 17:17 shows the word doing darker work, and it is worth pausing on. Divination and enchantment are described as things men used — instruments, techniques, methods for getting leverage over the future. That is the abiding appeal of the occult in every age, including this one, where it returns as astrology, manifestation, and the various therapeutic spiritualities. The biblical objection is not that such things never produce an effect but that they are an attempt to obtain from somewhere else what God has reserved to Himself, and the verse names the outcome plainly: sold themselves to do evil.
roots_summary: Hebrew damah (H1819), to liken, compare; nachash (H5172), to practise divination; Greek esan nesteuontes, were fasting; Latin uti, to employ.
roots_lines: Hebrew adammeh (H1819) — I will liken, use similitudes; Hosea 12:10, God's own account of His method.
Hebrew nechashim (H5172) — divinations, enchantments; 2 Kings 17:17, techniques for compelling the future.
Hebrew osheq (H6233) — oppression, extortion; Ezekiel 22:29, a practice the people of the land used.
Hebrew ger (H1616) — the stranger, sojourner; the party oppressed wrongfully in the same verse.
Latin uti, usus — to employ, employed; Webster's root behind both English senses.
usage: “I… used similitudes, by the ministry of the prophets” — accommodation in language, not fiction in fact.
“Used divination and enchantments” — the occult as technique, in any century.
“Used to fast” — the older English for were accustomed.

pos: pp. (drawn back; retired; taken away from a place or company)
etymology: From withdraw, from with in its old sense of away, against (as in withstand, withhold) and draw. To withdraw is to draw oneself away.
biblical_def: The word appears six times, and the subjects are strikingly varied: Christ, the Beloved, the LORD's hand, and a righteous man's hand. Luke uses it of Gethsemane: “And he was withdrawn from them about a stone's cast, and kneeled down, and prayed” (Luk 22:41) — near enough to be seen, far enough to be alone, which is the exact geometry of a man who wants his friends near and his Father nearer. The Song uses it of the felt absence of the Beloved: “I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer” (Son 5:6) — the classic text for what the Puritans called desertion, when the Lord hides His face from a true believer for a season. Lamentations uses it of judgment: “he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying” (Lam 2:8). And Ezekiel uses it of a just man's integrity: one “that hath withdrawn his hand from iniquity, hath executed true judgment between man and man” (Eze 18:8). Withdrawal in Scripture is therefore never neutral — it is either retreat for prayer, the withholding of comfort, the refusal to relent in judgment, or the pulling back of a hand from sin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines withdraw as to take back; to take from; to recall; and intransitively, to retire; to retreat; to quit a company or place.
webster_full: WITHDRAW', v.t. [with, to withdraw, and draw.]
1. To take back; to take from.
It is impossible that God should withdraw his presence from any thing.
2. To recall; to cause to retire or leave; to call back or away.
WITHDRAW', v.i. To retire; to retreat; to quit a company or place. He was withdrawn from them about a stone's cast. Luke 22.
scriptures: Luke 22:41
And he was withdrawn from them about a stone's cast, and kneeled down, and prayed,
Song of Solomon 5:6
I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.
Ezekiel 18:8
He that hath not given forth upon usury, neither hath taken any increase, that hath withdrawn his hand from iniquity, hath executed true judgment between man and man,
Lamentations 2:8

The LORD hath purposed to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion: he hath stretched out a line, he hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying: therefore he made the rampart and the wall to lament; they languished together.
corruption_summary: The experience of a withdrawn Lord is now diagnosed as depression or doubt, and the historic Reformed doctrine of desertion has been lost with it.
corruption_paragraphs: Song of Solomon 5:6 describes a believer who opened the door and found the Beloved gone — sought, called, and received no answer. The Puritans wrote at length about this and called it desertion, God withdrawing the sense of His favour from a soul He has not withdrawn His love from. The modern church has almost nothing to say about it, so a Christian in that condition is told he must have unconfessed sin, or is referred out for treatment of what is assumed to be a purely medical matter. Sometimes it is sin, and sometimes it is illness, and the church should say so in both cases. But sometimes it is neither, and the older divines knew it — Job and Heman and the Beloved's own bride are the evidence.

Lamentations 2:8 guards against the opposite sentimentality. There is a withdrawing God does not do: He had not withdrawn His hand from destroying Jerusalem, because the judgment was just and He had purposed it. A theology that can only speak of God drawing near, never of Him withholding, cannot read Lamentations at all. And Luke 22:41 supplies the pattern for the believer under either condition — withdrawn a stone's cast, kneeling, praying. The response to a hidden face is not to stop seeking it; the bride in the Song goes out into the streets at night looking.
roots_summary: Greek apospao (G645), to draw away; Hebrew chamaq (H2559), to turn away, withdraw; shub (H7725), to turn back.
roots_lines: Greek apespasthe (G645) — He was drawn away, torn away; Luke 22:41, a stronger verb than mere walking apart.
Hebrew chamaq (H2559) — to turn away, slip away; Song 5:6, of the Beloved gone from the door.
Hebrew heshib yado (H7725) — to turn back the hand; Ezekiel 18:8 of the just man, Lamentations 2:8 of the LORD in judgment.
Greek hos lithou bolen (G3037, G1000) — about a stone's cast; near enough to be watched, far enough to be alone.
Saxon with — away, against; the same prefix in withstand and withhold.
usage: “Withdrawn from them about a stone's cast” — friends near, Father nearer.
“My beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone” — the classic text on desertion.
“He hath not withdrawn his hand from destroying” — and that too is God.

pos: pp. (instructed; told; and in the legal sense, laid an accusation before an authority)
etymology: Latin informare, to shape, to form within, from in- and forma, form. To inform a man was first to form his mind; the courtroom sense came later, and the Authorized Version has both.
biblical_def: Six occurrences, and they divide cleanly between the two senses. Once it means instructed, and the instructor is an archangel: “And he informed me, and talked with me, and said, O Daniel, I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding” (Dan 9:22). Gabriel comes to shape Daniel's mind, and the sense is the older Latin one — forming within. The other five are legal, and every one of them concerns an accusation against Paul. “And they are informed of thee, that thou teachest all the Jews which are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses” (Act 21:21) — the charge circulating in Jerusalem, and false. “Ananias the high priest descended with the elders, and with a certain orator named Tertullus, who informed the governor against Paul” (Act 24:1) — a hired advocate laying a complaint. And Festus recalling it: “the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, desiring to have judgment against him” (Act 25:15). So the Bible's vocabulary of being informed runs from an angel giving understanding to a paid orator filing a charge, and the reader is meant to feel the distance between them.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inform as to instruct; to tell to; to acquaint; to communicate knowledge to; and, in law, to offer an accusation to a magistrate.
webster_full: INFORM', v.t. [L. informo; in and formo, to form.]
1. To animate; to give life to; to actuate by vital powers.
2. To instruct; to tell to; to acquaint; to communicate knowledge to.
He informed me, and talked with me. Dan. 9.
3. To offer an accusation to a magistrate against one; to communicate facts by way of accusation. He informed the governor against Paul. Acts 24.
scriptures: Daniel 9:22
And he informed me, and talked with me, and said, O Daniel, I am now come forth to give thee skill and understanding.
Acts 24:1
And after five days Ananias the high priest descended with the elders, and with a certain orator named Tertullus, who informed the governor against Paul.
Acts 21:21

And they are informed of thee, that thou teachest all the Jews which are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, saying that they ought not to circumcise their children, neither to walk after the customs.
Acts 25:15
About whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, desiring to have judgment against him.
corruption_summary: The informer's trade has been dignified as accountability, and a rumour repeated widely enough now functions as evidence.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 21:21 is worth reading slowly by anyone who has ever been the subject of a report. Paul was informed of — that is, a description of his teaching was circulating among thousands of believing Jews, and it was false. He had not taught the Jews to forsake Moses. The rumour was plausible, it travelled among sincere Christians, and it very nearly cost him his life. Ninth-commandment sins do not require malice to do their work; they require only that a report be repeated by people who assume somebody checked. The apostolic remedy in that chapter was a costly public demonstration of the truth, not a denial issued from a distance.

Acts 24:1 shows the professional version: Tertullus, an orator, retained to inform the governor. The trade of the paid accuser is older than the internet and now has better distribution. The distinction the church must keep is between the informer and the witness. Scripture requires witnesses — two or three, face to face, accountable, and liable to the same law if they lie (Deu 19:18-19) — and a charge against an elder is not even to be received except on that footing (1Ti 5:19). Anonymous accusation, however serious the matter, is the precise procedure the Bible refuses, and Daniel 9:22 stands at the other end of the word as a reminder of what informing is supposed to be: someone coming to give you skill and understanding.
roots_summary: Hebrew bin (H995), to discern, to cause to understand; Greek katecheo (G2727), to instruct by word of mouth; emphanizo (G1718), to lay information before a magistrate; Latin informare.
roots_lines: Hebrew wayyaben (H995) — and he gave understanding; Daniel 9:22, the angel forming the prophet's mind.
Greek katechethesan (G2727) — they were instructed, catechized; Acts 21:21, the rumour taught as fact.
Greek enephanisan (G1718) — they laid information, made a formal showing; Acts 24:1 and 25:15, the legal sense.
Greek rhetor (G4489) — an orator, a pleader; Tertullus, retained for the occasion.
Latin informare, from forma — to shape within; Webster's root, and the older English sense.
usage: “He informed me… to give thee skill and understanding” — informing at its best.
“They are informed of thee” — and the report was false.
“Tertullus, who informed the governor against Paul” — the paid accuser, an old trade.

pos: pp. (appointed; allotted; designated to a person or purpose)
etymology: Latin assignare, from ad- and signare, to mark — to mark out for someone. The word carries authority in it: only one with the right to allot can assign.
biblical_def: Three occurrences, and they show the word at three moral altitudes. At its best it is mercy institutionalized: “And on the other side Jordan by Jericho eastward, they assigned Bezer in the wilderness upon the plain out of the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead out of the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan out of the tribe of Manasseh” (Josh 20:8). These are cities of refuge, assigned by name and by tribe so that a man who killed without intent had somewhere to run before the avenger of blood reached him. God does not merely command mercy; He gives it a postal address. At its most ordinary it is statecraft: “the priests had a portion assigned them of Pharaoh, and did eat their portion which Pharaoh gave them” (Gen 47:22). And at its worst it is murder written as a duty roster: “And it came to pass, when Joab observed the city, that he assigned Uriah unto a place where he knew that valiant men were” (2Sa 11:16). Nothing in that sentence is illegal. A commander posted a soldier. The whole crime is hidden inside an administrative verb, which is exactly why David thought he could get away with it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines assign as to allot; to appoint or grant by distribution or apportionment; to designate or point out; and in law, to transfer or make over to another.
webster_full: ASSI'GNED, pp. Appointed; allotted; made over; shown or designated.
ASSI'GN, v.t. [L. assigno, ad and signo, to allot, from signum, a mark.]
1. To allot; to appoint or grant by distribution or apportionment.
The priests had a portion assigned them of Pharaoh. Gen. 47.
2. To designate or point out with precision; as, to assign a reason. 3. In law, to transfer, or make over to another.
scriptures: Joshua 20:8

And on the other side Jordan by Jericho eastward, they assigned Bezer in the wilderness upon the plain out of the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead out of the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan out of the tribe of Manasseh.
2 Samuel 11:16
And it came to pass, when Joab observed the city, that he assigned Uriah unto a place where he knew that valiant men were.
Genesis 47:22
Only the land of the priests bought he not; for the priests had a portion assigned them of Pharaoh, and did eat their portion which Pharaoh gave them: wherefore they sold not their lands.
Deuteronomy 19:10
That innocent blood be not shed in thy land, which the LORD thy God giveth thee for an inheritance, and so blood be upon thee.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that authority which assigns is accountable for what it assigns men to.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is plain and uncontested. What Scripture attaches to it, however, is a doctrine the age badly needs: that the man who assigns is answerable for the assignment. 2 Samuel 11:16 is the sharpest illustration in the Bible of a crime committed entirely through legitimate channels. Joab did not strike Uriah; he posted him. The order was lawful, the death was plausible, and the paperwork was clean. Nathan's indictment nonetheless goes to David: thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword of the children of Ammon. Distance through a chain of command does not distribute guilt away.

The principle to recover is the one Joshua 20:8 embodies. God assigned the cities of refuge by name, in reachable places, on both sides of Jordan, so that mercy was not left to good intentions. Deuteronomy gives the reason: that innocent blood be not shed in thy land. Authority in Scripture is always granted for the protection of the vulnerable, and any assignment — a posting, a portion, an allotment — is measured by whether it shelters the weak or exposes them. Joab and Joshua used the same verb; they will not receive the same verdict.
roots_summary: Hebrew hiqdish (H6942), to set apart, sanctify; choq (H2706), a portion decreed; pathan, to give over; Latin assignare, to mark out for.
roots_lines: Hebrew hiqdishu (H6942) — they set apart, consecrated; Joshua 20:8, the cities of refuge sanctified for that use.
Hebrew choq (H2706) — a decreed portion, allowance; Genesis 47:22, the priests' portion from Pharaoh.
Hebrew wayyitten — and he set, placed; 2 Samuel 11:16, Joab placing Uriah at the wall.
Hebrew go'el haddam (H1350, H1818) — the avenger of blood, whom the assigned cities existed to outrun.
Latin assignare, from ad- and signum — to mark out for someone; Webster's root.
usage: “They assigned Bezer… and Ramoth… and Golan” — mercy given a postal address.
“He assigned Uriah unto a place where he knew that valiant men were” — murder as a duty roster.
“A portion assigned them of Pharaoh” — the ordinary, administrative sense.

pos: v.t. (to keep back; to hold from proceeding; to hinder from going)
etymology: Latin detinere, from de- and tenere, to hold. To detain is to hold down or hold back — and the Bible's two occurrences are both about trying to hold an angel.
biblical_def: Both occurrences stand in the same conversation on the day Samson's birth was announced. Manoah, not yet knowing who his visitor was, pressed him to stay while a kid was made ready — ordinary Near Eastern hospitality offered to a stranger. The answer is the word's second occurrence and it is a gentle refusal with a redirection: “And the angel of the LORD said unto Manoah, Though thou detain me, I will not eat of thy bread: and if thou wilt offer a burnt offering, thou must offer it unto the LORD” (Jdg 13:16). The messenger will not take the meal a man wanted to give him; what may be given must go to the LORD, and Manoah's hospitality is converted into a sacrifice. That is a small and exact picture of the whole biblical ethic of worship — the impulse to honour is good, and its object must be corrected. The verb recurs in spirit elsewhere: Abraham's servant refusing delay, “Hinder me not, seeing the LORD hath prospered my way” (Gen 24:56); and Jacob at Peniel, holding on rather than holding back: “I will not let thee go, except thou bless me” (Gen 32:26). Man cannot detain God; he may, like Jacob, refuse to release Him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines detain as to keep back or from; to withhold; to keep what belongs to another; to keep or restrain from proceeding; and to hold in custody.
webster_full: DETA'IN, v.t. [L. detineo; de and teneo, to hold.]
1. To keep back or from; to withhold; to keep what belongs to another.
2. To keep or restrain from proceeding, either going or coming; to stay or stop.
Let us detain thee, until we shall have made ready a kid for thee. Judges 13.
3. To hold in custody. DETA'INER, n. One who withholds what belongs to another.
scriptures: Judges 13:16

And the angel of the LORD said unto Manoah, Though thou detain me, I will not eat of thy bread: and if thou wilt offer a burnt offering, thou must offer it unto the LORD. For Manoah knew not that he was an angel of the LORD.
Judges 13:19
So Manoah took a kid with a meat offering, and offered it upon a rock unto the LORD: and the angel did wondrously; and Manoah and his wife looked on.
Genesis 32:26
And he said, Let me go, for the day breaketh. And he said, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me.
Genesis 24:56
And he said unto them, Hinder me not, seeing the LORD hath prospered my way; send me away that I may go to my master.
corruption_summary: Manoah's instinct — to honour the messenger with what belonged to God — is the root of every creature-worship the Reformation had to undo.
corruption_paragraphs: Manoah meant well. He had met someone extraordinary and wanted to feed him, and the angel's refusal is the model for every faithful messenger since: if thou wilt offer a burnt offering, thou must offer it unto the LORD. The same refusal appears when John falls at the feet of the angel in Revelation and is told see thou do it not… worship God. The cult of the saints, the veneration of images, the elevation of the Virgin to a mediatorial office — all of it begins in Manoah's perfectly sincere hospitality, an honour offered to the bearer that belongs to the Sender. Rome distinguishes dulia from latria to license the practice; Judges 13:16 and Revelation 19:10 show what the messengers themselves think of the distinction.

The Protestant version of the error is the celebrity minister, and it is the same sin with worse manners. A congregation that could not be induced to bow before a statue will nonetheless build its faith on a man, defend him past the evidence, and grieve his fall as though a mediator had been lost. Judges 13:19 shows the right outcome: Manoah takes the kid he had meant for his visitor and offers it upon a rock unto the LORD — and then the wonder happens. The hospitality was not rebuked. It was redirected, and it was accepted where it belonged.
roots_summary: Hebrew atsar (H6113), to restrain, hold back, detain; shalach (H7971), to send away; Latin detinere, to hold down.
roots_lines: Hebrew na'tsar (H6113) — let us restrain, detain; Judges 13:15-16, the same root used of shutting up the heavens in 1 Kings 8:35.
Hebrew malak YHWH (H4397) — the angel of the LORD; the figure Manoah entertained without knowing.
Hebrew olah (H5930) — a burnt offering, that which goes up; what the hospitality became.
Hebrew shallechuni (H7971) — send me away; Genesis 24:56, the servant refusing to be detained.
Latin detinere, from de- and tenere — to hold down; Webster's root.
usage: “Though thou detain me, I will not eat of thy bread” — the messenger refusing what belongs to the Sender.
“Thou must offer it unto the LORD” — hospitality redirected, not rebuked.
“I will not let thee go, except thou bless me” — the one holding Scripture commends.

pos: v.t. (to carry or transport from one place to another; to escort safely)
etymology: Old French conveier, to accompany on the way, from Latin con- and via, a way — literally to go along the road with. The word's root is escort, not merely transport.
biblical_def: Both occurrences involve timber, kings, and the rebuilding of God's house. The first is Hiram of Tyre answering Solomon about the cedars: “My servants shall bring them down from Lebanon unto the sea: and I will convey them by sea in floats unto the place that thou shalt appoint me, and will cause them to be discharged there” (1Ki 5:9). Great logs lashed into rafts and floated down the coast to build the temple — a pagan king's shipping arrangement pressed into the service of the house of the LORD. The second is Nehemiah at the Persian court: “let letters be given me to the governors beyond the river, that they may convey me over till I come into Judah” (Neh 2:7). Here the older sense is exact — not freight but safe conduct, an escort under royal authority through hostile provinces. Nehemiah asks in the same breath for timber from the king's forest (Neh 2:8), which makes the parallel with Hiram complete. Twice the walls and the house of God are built with the resources and the roads of empires that did not worship Him, which is the doctrine of providence working through unbelieving hands.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines convey as to carry, bear or transport, by land or water; to pass or cause to pass; to transfer or make over; and to conduct or attend in the way.
webster_full: CONVEY', v.t. [L. conveho; con and veho, to carry.]
1. To carry, bear or transport, either by land or water, or in air.
I will convey them by sea in floats. 1 Kings 5.
2. To pass or cause to pass; to transmit; as, to convey a right or an estate from father to son.
3. To transfer; to pass a title to. 4. To impart; to communicate; as, to convey an idea. 5. To conduct or attend in the way; to escort.
scriptures: 1 Kings 5:9

My servants shall bring them down from Lebanon unto the sea: and I will convey them by sea in floats unto the place that thou shalt appoint me, and will cause them to be discharged there: and thou shalt accomplish my desire, in giving food for my household.
Nehemiah 2:7
Moreover I said unto the king, If it please the king, let letters be given me to the governors beyond the river, that they may convey me over till I come into Judah;
Nehemiah 2:8

And a letter unto Asaph the keeper of the king's forest, that he may give me timber to make beams for the gates of the palace which appertained to the house, and for the wall of the city, and for the house that I shall enter into. And the king granted me, according to the good hand of my God upon me.
Proverbs 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God routinely conveys His people and His materials by the hands of rulers who do not know Him.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word is ordinary and uncontested. What the two passages hold, though, is a doctrine the church keeps forgetting in both directions. Hiram was a Phoenician king with his own gods, and Artaxerxes was a Persian emperor; between them they supplied the cedar for the temple, the timber for the gates, and the safe conduct for Nehemiah. Neither man was converted, and both were instruments. Nehemiah's own comment on the transaction is the key: the king granted me, according to the good hand of my God upon me. He asked the king and he credited God, in one sentence, without embarrassment.

The principle to recover is confidence without either naivety or panic. One error treats a favourable ruler as a saviour and attaches the church's hopes to him; the other concludes that because the powers are unbelieving, nothing good can be conveyed through them. Proverbs 21:1 settles both: the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD… he turneth it whithersoever he will. Nehemiah prayed before he spoke to the king and asked plainly when he had the chance — and that combination, prayer and a plain request, is the whole method.
roots_summary: Hebrew sum (H7760), to set, place; ya'aviruni, from abar (H5674), to pass over; Latin convehere, to carry together; Old French conveier, to accompany on the way.
roots_lines: Hebrew dobroth (H1702) — floats, rafts; 1 Kings 5:9, the cedar lashed together for the sea passage.
Hebrew abar (H5674) — to pass over, cross; Nehemiah 2:7, that they may pass me over, the language of safe conduct.
Hebrew eber hannahar — beyond the river; the Persian satrapy Nehemiah had to cross.
Hebrew keyad elohai hattobah — according to the good hand of my God; Nehemiah's own footnote on the king's grant.
Latin con- and via — along the way with; the escort sense under the English word.
usage: “I will convey them by sea in floats” — a pagan king's shipping, building the temple.
“That they may convey me over” — safe conduct, not freight.
“According to the good hand of my God upon me” — asked the king, credited God.

pos: v.t. (to stretch out; to reach forth; to bestow or hold out to another)
etymology: Latin extendere, from ex- and tendere, to stretch. The picture is a hand or a line stretched out toward someone — which is why mercy and peace are the two things Scripture extends.
biblical_def: Both occurrences concern something stretched out toward a person, and the two are a study in contrast. The first is imprecation: “Let there be none to extend mercy unto him: neither let there be any to favour his fatherless children” (Psa 109:12). This is the severest of the imprecatory psalms, and the New Testament applies part of it to Judas. The petition asks that no hand be stretched out to a man who stretched out none — a plea that the measure a man used be measured to him, handed to the righteous Judge rather than executed by the psalmist. The second is the most generous promise in Isaiah: “Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the Gentiles like a flowing stream: then shall ye suck, ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees” (Isa 66:12). God stretches out peace like a river — not a cistern that can be drained but a current that keeps arriving — and the images that follow are of a nursing mother. The same book has already told Israel what forfeited it: “O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a river” (Isa 48:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines extend as to stretch in any direction; to carry forward or continue in length; to spread; to enlarge; and to bestow on, or impart to.
webster_full: EXTEND', v.t. [L. extendo; ex and tendo, to stretch.]
1. To stretch in any direction; to carry forward, or continue in length, as a line.
2. To spread in any direction; to expand; to enlarge in breadth.
3. To stretch; to reach forth; as, to extend the arm or hand.
4. To bestow on; to impart; to communicate. I will extend peace to her like a river. Is. 66. Let there be none to extend mercy unto him. Ps. 109.
scriptures: Isaiah 66:12

For thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the Gentiles like a flowing stream: then shall ye suck, ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees.
Psalm 109:12
Let there be none to extend mercy unto him: neither let there be any to favour his fatherless children.
Isaiah 48:18
O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a river, and thy righteousness as the waves of the sea:
Matthew 7:2
For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
corruption_summary: The imprecatory psalms are excised as sub-Christian, and the God who extends peace like a river is reduced to a God who extends nothing else.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 109 is among the psalms most often dropped from modern hymnals and lectionaries, on the ground that asking God to withhold mercy is beneath the Christian spirit. But the psalmist is not taking vengeance; he is refusing to take it, and handing the case to the only Judge entitled to try it. That is precisely what Romans 12:19 commands — avenge not yourselves… vengeance is mine, I will repay — and an imprecation is that command turned into a prayer. A church that cannot pray Psalm 109 has not become more merciful; it has generally become less honest, since the desire for justice does not disappear when it is denied the altar. It simply goes somewhere else.

The cost of cutting these psalms is that the other half of the word loses its weight. Isaiah 66:12 promises peace extended like a river, and the promise means something only because the God making it is the God of Psalm 109, who does in fact withhold. Mercy that cannot be withheld is not mercy but mechanism. And Isaiah 48:18 keeps the moral order visible: the river of peace was forfeited by a nation that would not hearken. The Reformed reading holds all three together — God extends peace freely to His own, He is just toward the impenitent, and the believer entrusts his enemies to Him rather than settling with them himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew natah (H5186), to stretch out, extend; mashak (H4900), to draw out, prolong; Latin extendere, to stretch out.
roots_lines: Hebrew noteh (H5186) — stretching out; Isaiah 66:12, peace extended like a river.
Hebrew mashak chesed (H4900, H2617) — to draw out lovingkindness; Psalm 109:12, the phrase rendered extend mercy.
Hebrew shalom kannahar (H7965, H5104) — peace like the river; a current, not a cistern.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — covenant lovingkindness; the mercy asked to be withheld, and the mercy God is full of.
Latin extendere, from tendere — to stretch; Webster's root, a hand held out.
usage: “I will extend peace to her like a river” — a current that keeps arriving.
“Let there be none to extend mercy unto him” — the case handed to the Judge, not settled by the psalmist.
“Then had thy peace been as a river” — the river was forfeited, not withheld arbitrarily.

pos: v.t. (to obtain; to bring about; to cause to come to one)
etymology: Latin procurare, to take care of, manage, from pro- and curare, to care for, from cura, care. To procure is to bring a thing about by taking pains over it.
biblical_def: Jeremiah has the word twice, and the two uses are the two directions a man's pains can run. The elders of the land defend Jeremiah by recalling Micah's case under Hezekiah, and conclude: “Thus might we procure great evil against our souls” (Jer 26:19). Killing the prophet would not merely be wrong; it would be a thing the killers brought upon themselves — procured, obtained, worked for. Sin in Scripture is frequently described this way, as a purchase a man makes with his own hands and then has to keep. The second use has God as the one taking pains: Jerusalem restored “shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and an honour before all the nations of the earth, which shall hear all the good that I do unto them: and they shall fear and tremble for all the goodness and for all the prosperity that I procure unto it” (Jer 33:9). God procures prosperity for a city He had just given over to the Chaldeans, and the nations tremble — not at the judgment, but at the goodness. Solomon states the general rule both ways: “He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour: but he that seeketh mischief, it shall come unto him” (Pro 11:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines procure as to get; to gain; to obtain, as by request, loan, effort, labor or purchase; to persuade or prevail on; and to cause; to bring on; to draw to.
webster_full: PROCU'RE, v.t. [L. procuro; pro and curo, to take care.]
1. To get; to gain; to obtain; as by request, loan, effort, labor or purchase.
We procure favor by kindness.
2. To persuade; to prevail on.
3. To cause; to bring on; to draw to; to attract. Thus might we procure great evil against our souls. Jer. 26.
scriptures: Jeremiah 33:9

And it shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and an honour before all the nations of the earth, which shall hear all the good that I do unto them: and they shall fear and tremble for all the goodness and for all the prosperity that I procure unto it.
Jeremiah 26:19

Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah put him at all to death? did he not fear the LORD, and besought the LORD, and the LORD repented him of the evil which he had pronounced against them? Thus might we procure great evil against our souls.
Proverbs 11:27
He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour: but he that seeketh mischief, it shall come unto him.
Galatians 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel has made procuring God's goodness a technique, while Jeremiah has God procuring it for a city that had earned the opposite.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 11:27 is the sort of verse the prosperity teachers build on — seek good and you shall procure favour — read as a mechanism a believer can operate. Proverbs states general wisdom, not a formula with a guarantee attached, and the same book that promises favour to the diligent also observes that the race is not always to the swift. More decisively, Jeremiah 33:9 puts God in the subject position: the prosperity that I procure unto it. The city could not procure it. The city had procured exile. When restoration comes, the nations tremble at goodness precisely because nobody can account for it on the basis of desert.

The opposite error is a fatalism that hears Jeremiah 33:9 and concludes that human pains are irrelevant, which Jeremiah 26:19 immediately blocks. The elders argue that killing a prophet would procure great evil against our souls — a real consequence, really brought about by a real choice, and their argument saved Jeremiah's life that day. Scripture holds both without strain: God procures what He gives, and men procure what they sow (Gal 6:7). A theology that drops either half produces either a magician or a spectator.
roots_summary: Hebrew asah (H6213), to do, make, bring about; biqqesh (H1245), to seek diligently; Latin procurare, to take care of.
roots_lines: Hebrew oseh lah (H6213) — that I do for it; Jeremiah 33:9, the prosperity God Himself brings about.
Hebrew osim ra'ah gedolah al naphshotenu — doing great evil against our souls; Jeremiah 26:19, sin as a thing worked for.
Hebrew shocher tob (H7836) — seeking good early and diligently; Proverbs 11:27.
Hebrew ratson (H7522) — favour, good pleasure; what the diligent seeker procures.
Latin procurare, from cura — care; Webster's root, to bring about by taking pains.
usage: “The prosperity that I procure unto it” — God in the subject position.
“Thus might we procure great evil against our souls” — sin as a purchase.
“He that diligently seeketh good procureth favour” — wisdom, not machinery.

pos: v.t. (to bear up; to uphold; to sustain, especially the weak)
etymology: Latin supportare, from sub-, under, and portare, to carry — literally to carry from underneath. The word is a picture of getting beneath a weight so another man need not carry all of it.
biblical_def: Both occurrences are apostolic commands, and both attach the word to the same object: the weak. Paul to the Ephesian elders, in his farewell at Miletus: “I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Act 20:35). Note that this is addressed to elders, and that Paul grounds it in his own manual labour — he had worked with his hands so that he could give rather than take, and he presents that as the pattern of eldership. Then to a whole congregation: “Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men” (1Th 5:14). Four different duties for four different people, and the discernment to tell them apart is itself a command. The unruly need warning, and the feebleminded need comfort, and to swap those treatments is to injure both. Supporting the weak is the same doctrine Paul elsewhere calls burden-bearing: “Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal 6:2); “We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves” (Rom 15:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines support as to bear; to sustain; to uphold; to endure without being overcome; to supply with means of living; and to sustain, as a person under trial.
webster_full: SUPPORT', v.t. [L. supporto; sub and porto, to carry.]
1. To bear; to sustain; to uphold; as, a prop or pillar supports a structure.
2. To endure without being overcome; as, to support pain or distress.
3. To sustain; to keep from fainting or sinking; as, to support the spirits.
4. To supply with means of living; to maintain. 5. To sustain; to assist. Ye ought to support the weak. Acts 20.
scriptures: Acts 20:35
I have shewed you all things, how that so labouring ye ought to support the weak, and to remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive.
1 Thessalonians 5:14
Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men.
Galatians 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
Romans 15:1
We then that are strong ought to bear the infirmities of the weak, and not to please ourselves.
corruption_summary: Support is either flattened into unconditional affirmation or outsourced entirely to programmes, and 1 Thessalonians 5:14 refuses both.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic sense of support has largely displaced the biblical one. To support a person now commonly means to affirm whatever he has decided, and to question him is treated as withdrawing support. 1 Thessalonians 5:14 makes that impossible to sustain from Scripture, because it lists warn them that are unruly in the same sentence. Paul assumes the church will do different things to different people according to what is actually wrong with them, and that discernment is the hard part. The disorderly man who is comforted is confirmed in his disorder; the feebleminded man who is warned is crushed. Getting it backwards is the commonest pastoral failure there is.

The second corruption is delegation. Support becomes a line item, a ministry, a referral — and the church can run a benevolence fund while no member actually gets under anyone's weight. Acts 20:35 pushes hard the other way: Paul's own calloused hands are exhibit A, and he is speaking to elders, telling them the leadership of a congregation is a giving office, not a receiving one. Galatians 6:2 names the standard it satisfies — so fulfil the law of Christ. Burden-bearing is not an optional ministry of mercy attached to the church; it is how the law of Christ gets kept.
roots_summary: Greek antilambanomai (G482), to take hold of in order to help; antechomai (G472), to hold firmly to; bastazo (G941), to bear a weight.
roots_lines: Greek antilambanesthai ton asthenounton (G482) — to take hold of, in place of, the weak; Acts 20:35, a hand under the arm.
Greek antechesthe ton asthenon (G472) — hold fast to the weak; 1 Thessalonians 5:14, the same duty with a grip in it.
Greek oligopsuchous (G3642) — the small-souled, fainthearted; the feebleminded who need comfort, not warning.
Greek ataktous (G813) — the disorderly, out of rank; a military word for the unruly who need warning.
Latin sub- and portare — to carry from underneath; Webster's root, and the whole picture.
usage: “Ye ought to support the weak” — said to elders, with calloused hands as the argument.
“Warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded” — and do not swap the treatments.
“Bear ye one another's burdens” — and so fulfil the law of Christ.
